prompt: The line graph below shows energy consumption in four countries from 1990 to 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
model:
The line graph compares how much energy was consumed in China, the USA, India and Russia between 1990 and 2020, measured in million tonnes.

Overall, consumption rose in three of the four countries, most dramatically in China, which replaced the USA as the largest consumer. Russia was the exception, as its figure barely changed over the thirty years.

In 1990, the USA used 2,100 million tonnes, more than twice as much as China (900) and Russia (850), while India consumed only 400. China's consumption then climbed steeply, reaching 1,900 million tonnes in 2005 and overtaking the American figure before 2010. By 2020 it had quadrupled to 3,600 million tonnes. India followed a similar but gentler path, more than tripling to 1,250 million tonnes and moving ahead of Russia after 2010.

By contrast, American consumption grew only slightly, reaching 2,450 million tonnes in 2020 after a small dip to 2,350 in 2010. Russia's figure fluctuated within a narrow band of 800 to 900 million tonnes and ended the period at 850, exactly where it had started.
notes: Band 7: the overview names the two key features (China overtaking the USA; Russia flat) and every figure matches the graph. Band 6 answers usually describe each line separately and miss the crossover.
band6: In 1990 the USA used 2,100 million tonnes, China used 900, Russia used 850 and India used 400. After that China increased very much and in 2020 China was 3,600, it is the biggest. India also increased to 1,250. The USA increased a little to 2,450 and Russia was 850.

criteria.tr: Overview selects the main trends and the China-USA crossover; figures are accurate; no reasons are invented. The band-6 version lists numbers without saying when China overtook the USA.
criteria.cc: Paragraphs group countries by trend (fast risers vs. stable); "then", "by contrast", "after a small dip" carry the timeline. The band-6 version links every clause with "and".
criteria.lr: Trend vocabulary is varied and precise: climbed steeply, quadrupled, more than tripling, fluctuated within a narrow band. The band-6 version repeats "increased".
criteria.gra: Mixes past perfect (had quadrupled), participle clauses (reaching..., overtaking...) and relative clauses (which replaced...). The band-6 version has a comma splice ("..., it is the biggest") and a tense slip.

prompt: The line graph below illustrates the percentage of internet users in three regions from 2000 to 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
model:
The line graph shows the percentage of people who used the internet in North America, Asia and Africa between 2000 and 2020.

Overall, internet use rose steadily in all three regions. North America had the highest rate throughout the period, but Asia grew the fastest, so the gap between these two regions narrowed considerably.

In 2000, 43% of North Americans were online, compared with just 2% of people in Asia and 0.5% in Africa. North American use increased quickly at first, reaching 78% in 2009, after which growth slowed; by 2020 the figure stood at 92%, almost the whole population.

Asia started very slowly, with only 10% online in 2006, but the rate then accelerated sharply. It rose to 35% in 2012 and doubled to 70% in 2020, a total increase of 68 percentage points, which was the largest of the three regions. As a result, the difference between Asia and North America fell from 41 points to 22. Africa remained well behind, with fewer than one in ten people online until 2012, when the figure was 8%. However, growth picked up after that, and by 2020 the African rate had reached 35%.
notes: Band 7: a clear overview (North America highest, Asia fastest, gap narrowing) and the distinction between percentage points and percentages. Band 6 answers often misreport growth or say North America "plateaued" when it rose 35 points.
band6: Asia was 2% in 2000 and it increased to 70% in 2020. It increased very fast. Africa was 0.5% and increased to 35%. North America was the highest, it was 43% and then 92%. So all regions increased.

criteria.tr: All three trends are covered, with the acceleration in Asia and Africa and the narrowing gap supported by figures. The band-6 version gives start and end points but no stages or comparison.
criteria.cc: Each detail paragraph covers one stage or region; "as a result" links the Asian surge to the narrowing gap. The band-6 version repeats "increased" and ends with a weak summary.
criteria.lr: Accurate use of "percentage points", "accelerated sharply", "picked up", "fewer than one in ten". The band-6 version uses one verb for every change.
criteria.gra: Relative clause (which was the largest), past perfect (had reached), time clauses. The band-6 version has a comma splice and only simple sentences.

prompt: The line graph below shows the average annual temperatures in two cities from 1980 to 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Average Annual Temperature in Two Cities (1980–2020)

model:
The line graph shows changes in the average annual temperature of Sydney and London between 1980 and 2020.

Overall, both cities became steadily warmer, and their temperatures rose by almost the same amount. Sydney remained far warmer than London throughout, with a gap of roughly twelve degrees.

In 1980, Sydney's average was 20.5°C, compared with only 8.2°C in London. Over the next two decades, temperatures in both cities increased gradually, reaching 21.2°C and 9.0°C respectively in 2000, which represents a rise of less than one degree in each case.

The increase was faster in the second half of the period, when the graph shows readings every five years. Between 2000 and 2020, both cities warmed by 1.1 degrees, so that Sydney reached 22.3°C and London 10.1°C. Although London started from a much lower base, its total rise of 1.9 degrees was marginally larger than Sydney's 1.8. As a result, the difference between the two cities narrowed very slightly, from 12.3 to 12.2 degrees.
notes: Band 7: the overview gives the shared trend and the constant gap; details compare the two halves of the period with exact differences. Band 6 answers often add causes such as global warming, which the graph does not show.
band6: Sydney was 20.5°C in 1980 and London was 8.2°C. Both cities temperature increased. In 2020 Sydney was 22.3°C and London was 10.1°C. This is because of global warming which is a big problem in the world.

criteria.tr: Accurate comparison of the two periods and of total change; no explanation is invented. The band-6 version adds a cause that is not in the data, which lowers Task Achievement.
criteria.cc: Clear progression from overview to first half to second half; "although" and "as a result" make the comparison explicit.
criteria.lr: Precise choices: marginally larger, from a much lower base, narrowed very slightly. The band-6 version has no comparative language.
criteria.gra: Concession (although), result clause (so that), relative clause (which represents). The band-6 version has a possessive error ("Both cities temperature").

prompt: The line graph below illustrates the number of mobile phone subscribers in four countries from 1995 to 2015. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Mobile Phone Subscribers in Four Countries (1995–2015)

model:
The line graph tracks how many people subscribed to mobile phone services in Japan, Germany, Brazil and Nigeria over the twenty years from 1995.

Overall, subscriptions grew enormously in all four countries. Japan and Germany adopted mobile phones earlier, but Brazil and Nigeria grew much faster later on and had overtaken both of them by 2015.

In 1995, numbers were tiny everywhere, ranging from 1.5 million in Japan to virtually none in Nigeria. Japan and Germany then expanded rapidly, reaching 87 and 65 million subscribers respectively in 2005, while Brazil had 35 million and Nigeria only 3 million. After this point, growth in the two early adopters slowed: Japan's total rose to 125 million in 2015 and Germany's to 110 million.

Brazil and Nigeria, in contrast, accelerated sharply after 2005. Brazil had overtaken Germany by 2010, when it had 86 million subscribers, and it finished the period as the leader with 145 million. Nigeria's rise was even more dramatic, as its figure jumped from 3 million to 54 million in five years and then to 140 million in 2015, which put it ahead of Japan as well.
notes: Band 7: groups the countries into early adopters and late, faster growers, and dates each overtaking correctly. Band 6 answers tend to describe four lines one after another and mix up the final ranking.
band6: Japan had 1.5 million in 1995 and 125 million in 2015. Germany had 0.3 million and 110 million. Brazil had 0.1 million and it grew to 145 million. Nigeria had 0 and it grew to 140 million. So all countries grew a lot.

criteria.tr: The overview names the reversal in ranking; details give the stage at which each change happened. The band-6 version reports only first and last values.
criteria.cc: Paragraph 3 covers the early adopters, paragraph 4 the late growers; "after this point", "in contrast" and "as well" tie them together.
criteria.lr: Range of trend verbs (expanded rapidly, accelerated sharply, jumped) and phrases (virtually none, early adopters).
criteria.gra: Past perfect (had overtaken), participle clause (ranging from...), non-defining relative clause. The band-6 version repeats one sentence pattern four times.

prompt: The bar chart below shows the number of international tourist arrivals in five Asian countries in 2015 and 2019. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: International Tourist Arrivals in Asian Countries (2015 & 2019)

model:
The bar chart compares the number of international tourists who arrived in five Asian countries in 2015 and 2019.

Overall, every country received more visitors in 2019 than in 2015. China was the most popular destination in both years, while Vietnam recorded the largest increase and rose from fourth to third place.

China welcomed 56.9 million international tourists in 2015, almost twice as many as Thailand, which had 29.9 million. Both countries grew over the four years, to 65.7 million and 39.8 million respectively. In absolute terms, Thailand's rise of 9.9 million was larger than China's 8.8 million, and proportionally it was more than double (33% compared with 15%).

The three smaller destinations attracted far fewer visitors. Vietnam's figure more than doubled, climbing from 8.0 million to 18.0 million, which meant that it overtook Indonesia, whose total increased from 10.2 million to 16.1 million. The Philippines remained the least visited country, although its arrivals still grew from 5.4 million to 8.3 million.
notes: Band 7: the overview states the leader and the biggest change; details compare absolute and proportional growth correctly. Band 6 answers often list ten numbers without comparing them.
band6: In 2015 China had 56.9 million tourists and in 2019 it had 65.7 million. Thailand had 29.9 million and 39.8 million. Vietnam had 8.0 million and 18.0 million. Indonesia had 10.2 million and 16.1 million. The Philippines had 5.4 million and 8.3 million.

criteria.tr: Key features (leader, fastest growth, change in ranking) are selected and supported. The band-6 version is a list with no overview and no comparison.
criteria.cc: Grouping into two large and three small destinations gives each paragraph a clear focus.
criteria.lr: Accurate comparison language: almost twice as many, in absolute terms, proportionally, the least visited.
criteria.gra: Relative clauses (which had..., whose total...) and a concession (although). The band-6 version uses only one structure.

prompt: The bar chart below presents household expenditure across six categories in the United Kingdom in 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
model:
The bar chart shows how much a UK household spent each week on six categories in 2010 and 2020.

Overall, spending went up in five of the six categories, and housing was by far the largest expense in both years. Transport was the only category in which spending fell.

Housing costs rose from £180 to £220 per week, an increase of 22%, and in both years this single category made up roughly half of the total weekly budget, which grew from £375 to £449. The sharpest proportional rise was in utilities, where spending went up by half, from £32 to £48. Food also became more expensive, increasing from £58 to £70, so that it overtook transport as the second-largest item.

Among the smaller categories, entertainment spending climbed from £25 to £35, while healthcare saw only a marginal rise, from £15 to £18. Transport, by contrast, decreased from £65 to £58 per week. It was therefore the only one of the six categories in which households spent less in 2020 than they had done ten years earlier.
notes: Band 7: picks out the largest item, the fastest-growing item and the single fall, with accurate totals. Band 6 answers often explain the fall in transport with reasons the chart does not give.
band6: Housing went up from £180 to £220. Transport went down from £65 to £58, maybe because people work from home. Food went up from £58 to £70 and utilities from £32 to £48. Entertainment and healthcare also went up.

criteria.tr: Every key feature is reported and supported; no causes are guessed. The band-6 version speculates ("maybe because people work from home").
criteria.cc: Paragraph 3 covers the large items, paragraph 4 the small items and the exception.
criteria.lr: Precise collocations: by far the largest expense, a marginal rise, the sharpest proportional rise.
criteria.gra: Relative clauses (in which, which grew), result clause (so that), past perfect. The band-6 version uses short simple sentences only.

prompt: The bar chart below shows carbon dioxide emissions from five sectors in a developed nation in 2015 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
model:
The bar chart compares carbon dioxide emissions from five sectors of a developed country's economy in 2015 and 2020.

Overall, emissions fell in four of the five sectors, with agriculture the only exception. Energy was the largest source in both years, and the ranking of the sectors did not change.

In 2015, the energy sector produced 280 megatonnes of CO₂, almost twice as much as transport (150 megatonnes). Industry was third at 120 megatonnes, followed by agriculture at 85 and waste at 45. Total emissions from the five sectors therefore stood at 680 megatonnes.

By 2020, the largest absolute cut had been made in energy, whose emissions dropped by 30 megatonnes to 250. Transport fell by 20 megatonnes to 130, which was the biggest proportional reduction at 13%. Smaller decreases were recorded in industry, down to 110 megatonnes, and waste, down to 40. Agricultural emissions, by contrast, rose slightly from 85 to 88 megatonnes, so the combined total for 2020 was 618 megatonnes.
notes: Band 7: notes that agriculture rose while all other sectors fell, and separates absolute from proportional change correctly. Band 6 answers often claim every sector decreased.
band6: All the sectors decreased between 2015 and 2020. Energy decreased from 280 to 250 and transport decreased from 150 to 130. Industry decreased from 120 to 110 and agriculture was 85 and 88. Waste decreased from 45 to 40.

criteria.tr: The exception (agriculture) is in the overview; figures and percentages are correct. The band-6 version states that all sectors fell, which the data contradicts.
criteria.cc: Paragraphs move from the 2015 ranking to the 2020 changes; "by contrast" marks the exception.
criteria.lr: Varied verbs and nouns for decrease: cut, dropped, fell, reduction, smaller decreases.
criteria.gra: Passives (had been made, were recorded), relative clauses (whose emissions, which was). The band-6 version repeats one verb in every clause.

prompt: The bar chart below illustrates the number of university degrees awarded to men and women in four countries during 2015 to 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
model:
The bar chart shows how many men and women graduated from university in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and Canada.

Overall, women earned more degrees than men in all four countries. The United States awarded far more degrees than the other three nations, while the gender gap was proportionally widest in the United Kingdom.

In the United States, 920,000 degrees were awarded to women, compared with 850,000 to men, a difference of 70,000. This was the largest gap in absolute terms, although it meant that women received only around 8% more degrees than men. In the United Kingdom, the figures were much lower, at 320,000 for women and 280,000 for men, yet the female lead of 40,000 represented a gap of about 14%.

Australia and Canada awarded similar numbers of degrees. Women in Australia received 160,000 degrees, while men received 145,000, and the corresponding figures for Canada were 140,000 and 125,000. In both countries, therefore, women were ahead by 15,000, which was a gap of 10% in Australia and 12% in Canada.
notes: Band 7: compares absolute and proportional gaps and gets every percentage right. Band 6 answers often explain the gap (for example "women study harder"), which is opinion, not data.
band6: In all countries women got more degrees than men. In the USA women got 920 and men got 850. In the UK women got 320 and men 280. In Australia and Canada women also got more. This shows women are more interested in education now.

criteria.tr: Key comparisons are quantified and correct; nothing is added that the chart does not show. The band-6 version drops the unit (thousands) and adds an opinion.
criteria.cc: Paragraph 3 covers the two largest systems, paragraph 4 the two similar ones; "yet", "therefore" and "the corresponding figures" link the comparisons.
criteria.lr: Comparison phrases: in absolute terms, proportionally widest, the female lead, the corresponding figures.
criteria.gra: Passive (were awarded), concession (although, yet), relative clause (which was a gap). The band-6 version has only simple sentences.

prompt: The table below provides data on internet usage and smartphone ownership among different age groups in 2019 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

chart.title: Internet and Smartphone Usage by Age Group (2019 & 2024)

model:
The table gives the percentages of four age groups who used the internet and owned a smartphone in 2019 and 2024.

Overall, both internet use and smartphone ownership rose in every age group, and in both years the figures fell as age increased. The fastest growth was among the oldest groups, so the generational gap narrowed.

Internet use was already almost universal among 16-24-year-olds in 2019, at 95%, and it edged up to 98% in 2024. The 25-44 group showed a similar pattern, rising from 88% to 94%. By contrast, only 45% of people aged 65 and over were online in 2019, but this proportion grew by 17 percentage points to 62%, while the figure for those aged 45-64 increased from 72% to 83%.

Smartphone ownership was consistently lower than internet use, and the difference was greatest for older people. In 2019, 92% of the youngest group owned a smartphone, compared with just 18% of those over 65. Five years later, the over-65 figure had nearly doubled to 35%, and ownership among 45-64-year-olds had risen from 52% to 68%. The two youngest groups recorded smaller gains, reaching 96% and 87%.
notes: Band 7: two overview points (falls with age; fastest growth among older groups) and accurate percentage-point changes. Band 6 answers often confuse percentage points with per cent or say a figure "doubled" when it did not.
band6: Young people use the internet most. In 2019, 95% of 16-24 used internet and in 2024 98%. Old people were 45% and 62%, it more than doubled. Smartphone is the same, young people have more smartphones than old people.

criteria.tr: Both measures and all four groups are covered with correct figures. The band-6 version makes a factual error (45% to 62% is not "more than doubled").
criteria.cc: Paragraph 3 = internet, paragraph 4 = smartphones; inside each, young groups then old groups.
criteria.lr: Precise phrases: almost universal, edged up, percentage points, nearly doubled.
criteria.gra: Past perfect, participle clauses and comparison structures (consistently lower than). The band-6 version has a comma splice and missing articles.

prompt: The table below shows global water usage by sector in 2010 and 2020, measured in cubic kilometres per year. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
model:
The table shows how much water was used globally by four sectors in 2010 and 2020, measured in cubic kilometres.

Overall, water use increased in all four sectors over the decade. Agriculture was by far the largest user in both years, consuming more than the other three sectors combined.

In 2010, agriculture accounted for 2,660 km³ of the 4,610 km³ used in total, which is roughly 58%. Its consumption rose by 180 km³ to 2,840 km³ in 2020, the largest absolute increase of any sector. Even so, its share of total use fell slightly, to about 57%, since the other sectors grew at a slightly faster rate.

Industry was the second-largest user, and its consumption went up from 850 km³ to 920 km³. Hydropower followed a similar trend, rising from 720 km³ to 780 km³, while municipal use, which was the smallest category, increased from 380 km³ to 410 km³. Taken together, global water use grew by 340 km³, or around 7%, to reach 4,950 km³ by 2020.
notes: Band 7: calculates shares and totals correctly and links them to the main feature (agriculture larger than the rest combined). Band 6 answers often list each row with no total or share.
band6: Agriculture used 2,660 in 2010 and 2,840 in 2020. Industry used 850 and 920. Municipal used 380 and 410. Hydropower used 720 and 780. All sectors increased, agriculture is the biggest.

criteria.tr: Overview and details are supported by correct calculations (58%, 57%, 7%). The band-6 version omits units and offers no overview sentence.
criteria.cc: Paragraph 3 explains the dominant sector, paragraph 4 the others and the total; "even so" and "taken together" guide the reader.
criteria.lr: Range: accounted for, the largest absolute increase, share of total use, followed a similar trend.
criteria.gra: Passive (was used), relative clause, participle clause (consuming..., rising...).

prompt: The table below presents data on educational attainment levels among the working-age population in three countries for 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
model:
The table compares the highest level of education reached by working-age adults in Germany, Brazil and India in 2010 and 2020.

Overall, the proportion of people with only primary education fell in all three countries, while the share with a university degree rose. Germany had by far the most highly educated population and India the least, although Brazil and India changed far more over the decade.

In Germany, almost everyone had gone beyond primary school, with just 3% in this category in 2010 and 2% in 2020. Tertiary graduates increased from 45% to 50% and overtook those whose highest level was secondary education, which declined from 52% to 48%.

Brazil and India both saw major shifts. In Brazil, the primary-only group shrank by 16 percentage points to 28%, and secondary education became the most common level, rising from 42% to 50%. University graduates also grew, from 14% to 22%. In India, primary-only education remained the largest category, but it dropped by the same 16 points, from 68% to 52%. Over the same period, the share with secondary education rose from 22% to 35%, while tertiary graduates increased only slightly, from 10% to 13%.
notes: Band 7: an overview that compares countries and directions of change, then country-by-country detail with correct point changes. Band 6 answers often call a fall from 44% to 28% "halved".
band6: In Germany primary was 3% and 2%, secondary was 52% and 48% and tertiary was 45% and 50%. In Brazil primary halved from 44% to 28%. In India primary was 68% and 52%. All countries improved their education.

criteria.tr: Overview covers both the shared trend and the differences between countries. The band-6 version contains a factual error ("halved").
criteria.cc: Germany in one paragraph, Brazil and India together because they changed the most; "both", "over the same period" and "while" connect them.
criteria.lr: Accurate terms: tertiary graduates, primary-only, percentage points, shrank, overtook.
criteria.gra: Relative clauses (whose highest level..., which declined...), past perfect, participle clause.

prompt: The pie chart below illustrates the distribution of global smartphone operating system market share in 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features.
model:
The pie chart shows how the global smartphone market was divided between operating systems in 2024.

Overall, the market was dominated by just two systems, Android and iOS, which together accounted for 99% of all smartphones. Android was clearly the leader, with a share more than twice as large as that of its rival.

Android held 72% of the market, which means that almost three out of every four smartphones ran this system. iOS was in second place with 27%, a little over a quarter of the total. The gap between the two leaders was therefore 45 percentage points, and Android's share was more than two and a half times that of iOS.

All the remaining operating systems were grouped together in the chart as 'Other', and their combined share was only 1%. In other words, for every hundred smartphones, around ninety-nine used one of the two main systems, while just one used an alternative. The market was therefore highly concentrated, since no third system held a meaningful share of the total.
notes: Band 7: with only three slices, the answer earns its marks by expressing proportions accurately (three out of four, a little over a quarter) and comparing them, not by explaining why Android leads. Band 6 answers often pad the answer with reasons and brand opinions.
band6: Android is 72% and iOS is 27% and other is 1%. Android is the biggest because it is cheaper and many companies make Android phones. iOS is only for Apple phones so it is less. Other is very small.

criteria.tr: Every figure is reported and compared; no causes are invented. The band-6 version spends half its words on reasons that are not in the chart.
criteria.cc: Leader and runner-up in one paragraph, the remainder in the next; "therefore" and "in other words" draw conclusions from the numbers.
criteria.lr: Proportion language: almost three out of every four, a little over a quarter, combined share, highly concentrated.
criteria.gra: Relative clauses and comparatives (more than twice as large as that of...).

prompt: The pie chart below shows the composition of global carbon dioxide emissions by source in 2023. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features.
model:
The pie chart illustrates the proportion of global carbon dioxide emissions that came from five sources in 2023.

Overall, energy production was the largest source by a wide margin, and three sectors, namely energy production, transportation and manufacturing, were responsible for the great majority of emissions. Waste management contributed the smallest share.

Energy production generated 41% of all emissions, which was considerably more than any other source and close to the combined share of the next two. Transportation ranked second at 24%, roughly a quarter of the total, and manufacturing was only slightly lower at 21%. Taken together, these three sources accounted for 86% of global emissions.

The two remaining sources were much less significant. Agriculture produced 11%, around half the figure for manufacturing, while waste management accounted for only 3%, the smallest proportion in the chart. In fact, the share of energy production alone was nearly four times that of agriculture and more than thirteen times that of waste management.
notes: Band 7: a ranked, grouped description with accurate proportions and no policy advice. Band 6 answers often turn Task 1 into an essay about solutions to climate change.
band6: Energy production is 41%, it is the most. Transportation is 24% and manufacturing is 21%. Agriculture is 11% and waste management is 3%. So governments must reduce energy production emissions to stop climate change.

criteria.tr: All five sources are reported, grouped and compared. The band-6 version ends with a recommendation, which is not part of Task 1.
criteria.cc: Big three in one paragraph, small two in the next; "taken together" and "in fact" add comparison.
criteria.lr: Range: by a wide margin, namely, responsible for the great majority, much less significant.
criteria.gra: Relative clauses, comparatives (nearly four times that of...), varied sentence openings.

prompt: The process diagram below illustrates the stages involved in producing paper from raw timber. Summarise the information and describe the main steps of the process.

chart.title: Paper Production Process from Raw Timber
steps: Raw timber logs are delivered to the paper mill and are de-barked to remove outer bark
The de-barked wood is chipped into small pieces using industrial chipping machines
The wood chips are treated with chemicals in digesters to break down the lignin and separate fibres
The resulting pulp mixture is bleached and cleaned to remove impurities and achieve desired whiteness
The cleaned pulp is pressed and dried using heated rollers to reduce moisture content to approximately 5–8%
The dried paper sheets are calendered to achieve smoothness and consistent thickness before being rolled or cut into final products

model:
The diagram shows the stages by which paper is produced from raw timber.

Overall, there are six main stages in the process, beginning with the delivery of logs to a paper mill and ending with finished paper that is ready to be rolled or cut. The process combines mechanical steps, such as chipping and pressing, with a chemical treatment stage.

First, raw timber logs are delivered to the mill, where their outer bark is removed. The de-barked wood is then cut into small chips by industrial chipping machines. In the third stage, these chips are treated with chemicals in large containers called digesters, which break down the lignin and separate the wood fibres. The resulting pulp is subsequently bleached and cleaned so that impurities are removed and the desired whiteness is achieved.

Once the pulp has been cleaned, it is pressed and dried by heated rollers until its moisture content falls to approximately 5-8%. Finally, the dried sheets are calendered, a process which makes them smooth and of consistent thickness, before they are either rolled or cut into final products.
notes: Band 7: every stage in order, with the passive voice and sequence markers, and an overview that gives the number of stages and the start and end points. Band 6 answers often copy the step labels and drop the overview.
band6: First, the logs come to the mill and remove the bark. Then the wood is chip into small pieces. Then chemicals break the wood. Then the pulp is bleach and clean. Then it is dry. Then it is calendered and cut.

criteria.tr: All six stages included with the key detail (moisture 5-8%); overview states start, end and number of stages. The band-6 version has no overview.
criteria.cc: Sequence markers vary (first, then, in the third stage, subsequently, once, finally). The band-6 version uses "then" five times.
criteria.lr: Process vocabulary: de-barked, digesters, pulp, moisture content, calendered.
criteria.gra: Consistent, accurate passives and a time clause (Once the pulp has been cleaned). The band-6 version has passive form errors ("is chip", "is bleach") and a wrong active ("the logs ... remove the bark").

prompt: The process diagram below shows the stages in the recycling of plastic waste into new products. Summarise the information and describe the main steps of the process.

chart.title: Plastic Waste Recycling Process
steps: Plastic waste is collected from households and commercial sources through recycling bin programmes
Collected plastic is transported to recycling centres where it is sorted by plastic type (PET, HDPE, PVC, LDPE, PP, PS, Other)
Sorted plastic is shredded into small flakes to increase surface area and improve processing efficiency
Plastic flakes are washed thoroughly to remove contaminants, labels, and adhesives
Cleaned plastic flakes are melted in industrial furnaces at high temperatures to form molten plastic
The molten plastic is extruded through dies to form plastic pellets or granules of uniform size
Plastic pellets are sold to manufacturers who mould them into new products such as containers, textiles, or building materials

model:
The diagram illustrates how plastic waste is recycled and turned into new products.

Overall, the process consists of seven stages. It begins with the collection of waste from homes and businesses and ends when recycled pellets are sold to manufacturers, who mould them into new goods.

At the start of the process, plastic waste is collected from households and commercial sources through recycling bin programmes. It is then transported to recycling centres, where it is sorted according to type, for example PET, HDPE or PVC. After sorting, the material is shredded into small flakes, which increases its surface area, and these flakes are washed thoroughly so that contaminants, labels and adhesives are removed.

In the next stage, the clean flakes are melted in industrial furnaces at high temperatures. The molten material is then forced through dies in a process called extrusion, which produces pellets or granules of a uniform size. Finally, these pellets are sold to manufacturers, who use them to make a range of new products such as containers, textiles and building materials.
notes: Band 7: seven stages in order, passive throughout, overview with start and end points. Band 6 answers often add opinions about the environment at the end.
band6: People put plastic in recycling bins and trucks take it to the centre. Workers sort the plastic. Then they cut it and wash it. Then they melt it and make pellets. This process is very good for the environment and everyone should recycle.

criteria.tr: All seven stages and the purpose of each (sorting by type, shredding to increase surface area) are given. The band-6 version invents actors and ends with an opinion.
criteria.cc: Two detail paragraphs split the process in the middle; markers include at the start, after sorting, in the next stage, finally.
criteria.lr: Accurate technical words: contaminants, adhesives, molten, extrusion, granules.
criteria.gra: Passives, non-defining relative clauses (which increases..., who use...), purpose clause (so that).

prompt: The map below shows the development of a coastal city between 1990 and 2020. Summarise the information and describe the main changes that have occurred.

features: Small harbour in the south with fishing docks
Historic town centre with low-rise buildings (2–3 storeys) clustered in the middle
Residential areas scattered to the north and east
Dense mangrove forest to the north
Agricultural fields occupying western and southern peripheries
Single main road connecting harbour to town centre
Expanded modern port facility with container terminals, now covering triple the original area
High-rise commercial and residential development in town centre (10+ storey buildings)
Extensive suburban sprawl northward and eastward with residential estates
Mangrove forest significantly reduced to scattered patches, largely cleared for development
Agricultural fields largely replaced by housing and industrial zones
Network of multi-lane highways and ring roads replacing original single road
Significantly expanded airport with new terminals and extended runways

model:
The map shows how a coastal city changed between 1990 and 2020.

Overall, the city was transformed from a small, low-rise town surrounded by countryside into a large, densely built urban area. This growth took place largely at the expense of farmland and the mangrove forest, while transport facilities were greatly expanded.

In 1990, the town had a small harbour with fishing docks in the south, and a single main road linked it to the historic centre, where buildings were only two or three storeys high. Housing was scattered to the north and east, a dense mangrove forest covered the north, and farmland occupied the western and southern edges.

By 2020, the harbour had been expanded into a modern container port covering three times its original area, and the centre had been redeveloped with buildings of ten storeys or more. Residential estates had spread northwards and eastwards, while the mangrove forest had been cleared to scattered patches and most of the farmland had been replaced by housing and industrial zones. The single road had given way to a network of multi-lane highways and ring roads, and the small eastern airport had been enlarged with new terminals and longer runways.
notes: Band 7: a then-and-now structure with the past perfect passive for changes and an overview of the big picture (urbanisation at the expense of nature). Band 6 answers often explain why the city grew, which the map does not show.
band6: In 1990 there was a small harbour, a town centre and farms. There was a forest in the north and an airport. In 2020 the harbour is bigger and there are tall buildings. The forest is cut because the city needs more houses. The airport is bigger.

criteria.tr: All main features are compared across the two years; nothing is explained beyond the map. The band-6 version adds a reason and misses the roads and farmland.
criteria.cc: One paragraph per year, each moving around the map in a similar order so changes are easy to match.
criteria.lr: Map vocabulary: low-rise, redeveloped, residential estates, given way to, scattered patches.
criteria.gra: Past perfect passive (had been expanded, had been enlarged) used accurately. The band-6 version mixes present and past tense.
